question: Which is better for most knowledge jobs: remote work or office work?
subject: remote versus office work
ladder: That doesn't match the evidence. Microsoft's study of 61,000 employees found cross-team collaboration dropped sharply under full remote and never recovered over the following two years.
The Stanford result you're probably thinking of was call-center staff doing repetitive scripted work. Bloom himself said in the follow-up that it doesn't generalize to open-ended knowledge work.
Meta, Google, Amazon, Dell and Salesforce all reversed remote policies after internal productivity audits. Five independent firms with different cultures reached the same conclusion.

A meta-analysis across 47 studies found remote work cuts mentorship transfer to junior staff by about a third. That compounds year over year and doesn't show up in one-year productivity numbers at all.
The apparent productivity gains mostly vanish once you control for hours worked. Remote staff log more hours for the same output — that's not a gain, that's unpaid overtime.

question: Is nuclear power a good way to decarbonize electricity?
side_a: Yes, nuclear is a good route
side_b: No, nuclear is not a good route
subject: nuclear power as a decarbonization route
ladder: The cost trend goes the wrong way. Lazard's levelized cost analysis has nuclear rising while solar and wind fell by roughly 90% over the same period.
Vogtle came in seven years late and more than double budget. Flamanville and Hinkley Point C followed the same pattern. Three projects, three continents, same overrun.
Build time is the killer. The median reactor takes about a decade from approval to grid. Utility-scale solar takes eighteen months. On a 2035 deadline, one of those is a real option and one isn't.
Germany and Japan both scaled nuclear back and still cut emissions, because the displaced capital went into renewables that deployed faster per dollar.
Every dollar in nuclear is a dollar not in storage or transmission, which are the actual bottlenecks. The opportunity cost argument is what most energy economists now lead with.

question: Should universities require standardized test scores?
subject: standardized testing requirements in university admissions
ladder: The predictive validity is weaker than usually claimed. Once you control for high school GPA, test scores add only a few percentage points of explained variance in first-year performance.
The score-income gradient is nearly monotonic across brackets. That's not measuring aptitude, that's measuring access to preparation.
The University of California system commissioned its own faculty review, and the outcome was to drop the requirement entirely. That was an internal study by people who wanted to keep it.
Test-optional institutions saw applicant diversity rise without measurable declines in graduation rates. If the tests were doing selection work, that shouldn't happen.
The prep industry is a multi-billion dollar market built entirely on the fact that scores are coachable. A coachable measure is not measuring what it claims to measure.

question: Should companies move to a four-day work week?
subject: the four-day work week
ladder: The UK pilot that gets cited had companies self-select into it and self-report the outcomes. That's the weakest possible design for a productivity claim.
Most trials compress the same hours into fewer days rather than reducing them. Reported wellbeing gains sit alongside longer, denser days.
It only works for output measured in discrete deliverables. Coverage-based work — clinical, support, operations — has to hire to fill the gap, which shifts cost rather than removing it.
Iceland's trial is described as covering the national workforce, but it was about 1% of workers, mostly in office roles, with no productivity measurement at all.
Firms that ran it for more than eighteen months quietly reverted at a high rate. Short pilots capture a novelty effect that doesn't survive.

question: Is household recycling worth the effort it requires?
side_b: No, it is not worth it
subject: household recycling
ladder: Only a small single-digit share of plastic ever produced has actually been recycled. The rest was landfilled, burned, or exported.
After China's import restrictions, a large fraction of collected material had no destination and went straight to landfill — collected, sorted, then dumped.
Contamination rates in single-stream systems run high enough that entire loads get rejected. One dirty container can void a whole batch.
Internal industry documents show manufacturers promoted recycling while knowing most plastics were uneconomical to reprocess. It was a marketing program, not a waste strategy.
The lifecycle accounting rarely includes collection trucks, sorting facilities, and ocean freight. Once you add them, several material streams come out net negative.

question: Should restaurant tipping be replaced by higher fixed wages?
subject: replacing tipping with higher fixed wages
ladder: The restaurants that tried it mostly reverted. Danny Meyer's group ran no-tipping for years across multiple venues and reversed the whole policy.
Tipped staff opposed it most strongly. Servers in high-volume rooms lost income under fixed wages, and turnover went up rather than down.
Menu prices have to rise visibly to fund it, and customers respond to the sticker rather than the total. Covers dropped at venues that made the switch.
It compresses the gap between kitchen and front-of-house pay, which sounds fair, but it removed the earnings ceiling that kept experienced servers in the job.
Research on tip variance finds it correlates only weakly with service quality — but weak correlation is still more performance linkage than a flat wage provides.
